facts: The Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip in the northeast, was created in the 19th century as a buffer so the Russian and British empires would not share a border.
Afghanistan is landlocked and mountainous, with the Hindu Kush running through its centre.
It is one of the world's largest producers of lapis lazuli, mined in Badakhshan for more than 6,000 years.
AF.about: Set where Central Asia, South Asia and the Iranian Plateau meet, Afghanistan has been a crossroads for traders and armies since antiquity, from Alexander the Great to the caravans of the Silk Road. Its rivers mostly drain inland: the Amu Darya traces the northern frontier, while the Helmand flows south-west into the marshes and salt flats of the Sistan basin, crossing the Registan and Dasht-e Margo deserts on the way. Summers are hot and dry, winters bitter in the highlands. The modern state is usually traced to the Durrani Empire founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747, and full control of foreign affairs was secured from Britain in 1919. Since 1979 the country has endured Soviet intervention, civil war and repeated changes of regime. Most Afghans still live in rural villages and depend on farming and herding, and the population includes Pashtuns, Tajiks, Hazaras and Uzbeks, with Dari and Pashto the main languages.

facts: Armenia was the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion, traditionally dated to 301.
Mount Ararat is its national symbol and appears on the coat of arms, though the mountain lies inside Turkey.
The Armenian alphabet was created around 405 and is still used essentially unchanged.
AM.about: Armenia occupies a rugged volcanic upland in the South Caucasus, and almost all of its territory lies above 1,000 metres. Lake Sevan, in the east, is one of the largest high-altitude freshwater lakes in the world and a vital source of water and fish. The region is seismically active, and the Spitak earthquake of 1988 killed around 25,000 people. Armenian kingdoms reached their greatest extent under Tigranes the Great in the first century BC, but for most of the following two millennia the Armenian homeland was divided between rival empires. During the First World War, Armenians in the Ottoman Empire suffered mass killings and deportations. A short-lived republic in 1918 was followed by seven decades of Soviet rule, and independence came in 1991. Long conflict with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh ended in 2023 when Azerbaijan took full control of the region. A large global diaspora, bigger than the population at home, remains central to the nation's economy and identity.

facts: Baku sits about 28 metres below sea level, making it the lowest-lying national capital in the world.
The world's first industrially drilled oil well was sunk near Baku in 1846.
Azerbaijan borders Turkey only through Nakhchivan, an exclave separated from the rest of the country by Armenia.
AZ.about: Stretched between the Greater Caucasus and the western shore of the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan packs snowy peaks, subtropical lowlands and semi-desert into a fairly compact territory. The Kura River crosses a broad central plain on its way to the Caspian, and the Absheron Peninsula juts out into the sea. The country has hundreds of mud volcanoes, more than almost anywhere else on Earth, and the rock carvings of Gobustan record human life here over thousands of years. In 1918 the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic became one of the first parliamentary republics in the Muslim world, but it was absorbed into the Soviet Union in 1920; independence followed in 1991. Oil and natural gas dominate the economy, exported westward through pipelines such as the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan line, opened in 2006. Azerbaijani is a Turkic language closely related to Turkish, and most of the population is Shia Muslim, though the state is constitutionally secular.

facts: Bahrain is an archipelago of about 50 natural islands plus dozens more created by land reclamation.
It was the first country in the Persian Gulf to discover oil, in 1932, and the first to begin diversifying away from it.
The King Fahd Causeway has linked it by road to Saudi Arabia since 1986.
BH.about: Low, flat and surrounded by the shallow waters of the Gulf, Bahrain was the centre of Dilmun, a Bronze Age trading civilisation that linked Mesopotamia with the Indus Valley. Thousands of ancient burial mounds still cover parts of the main island and are now listed by UNESCO. Freshwater springs, some bubbling up from the seabed, once made the islands an unusually green oasis, and for centuries the economy revolved around pearl diving in the surrounding oyster beds, a tradition also recognised by UNESCO. The ruling Al Khalifa family has governed since the late 18th century, and Bahrain was a British protectorate until it became fully independent in 1971. Today it is a regional centre for banking and finance and hosts a Formula One Grand Prix. Foreign workers make up roughly half of the population, and the country is a constitutional monarchy.

facts: Bangladesh sits on the world's largest river delta, formed by the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna.
It is among the most densely populated countries on Earth, with more people than Russia in a fraction of the space.
The Sundarbans, shared with India, is the largest mangrove forest in the world and a stronghold of the Bengal tiger.
BD.about: Flat, fertile and laced with hundreds of rivers, Bangladesh lies mostly just a few metres above sea level, so the annual monsoon shapes almost every aspect of life. Seasonal floods renew the soil that supports intensive rice farming, while cyclones from the Bay of Bengal pose a recurring threat to the coast. The only significant hills are in the Chittagong Hill Tracts in the south-east, and Cox's Bazar has one of the longest natural sandy beaches in the world. The region was part of British India until 1947, when partition made it East Pakistan. Resentment over language and political power grew, and the 1952 Language Movement, defending Bengali, is now remembered worldwide as International Mother Language Day on 21 February. After the Liberation War of 1971, Bangladesh became independent. Its economy has grown rapidly since, driven above all by garment manufacturing, in which it ranks among the world's largest exporters, and by remittances from workers abroad.

facts: Bhutan measures progress by Gross National Happiness alongside economic output.
Its constitution requires at least 60% of the country to remain under forest cover; the actual figure is higher.
Gangkhar Puensum is the highest unclimbed mountain in the world, as climbing above 6,000 metres is prohibited.
BT.about: Climbing from subtropical foothills near the Indian plains to glaciated Himalayan peaks above 7,000 metres, Bhutan crosses an extraordinary range of climates within a short distance. Fast rivers cut deep north–south valleys, and these valleys hold most of the towns, farms and the fortress-monasteries known as dzongs. The country was unified in the 17th century by the Tibetan lama Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, who established a state shaped by Drukpa Kagyu Buddhism. The Wangchuck dynasty has reigned since 1907, and Bhutan was never colonised, though it conducted foreign relations under treaties first with Britain and later with India. Television and the internet were only permitted in 1999. In 2008 the monarchy voluntarily became constitutional and the first parliamentary elections were held. Hydropower sold to India is the largest source of export earnings, and tourism is deliberately limited through a daily fee, reflecting a policy of attracting fewer, higher-spending visitors.

facts: Brunei is split into two parts, both surrounded by the Malaysian state of Sarawak.
Oil and gas wealth means citizens pay no income tax and receive free healthcare and education.
Around 70% of the country is still covered by rainforest, one of the highest proportions in Asia.
BN.about: On the northern coast of Borneo, facing the South China Sea, Brunei has a hot, humid equatorial climate and a landscape of coastal swamps, rivers and forested hills. Its sultanate was once a major regional power: in the 15th and 16th centuries it held sway over much of Borneo's coastline and parts of the southern Philippines. Territory was lost steadily in the 19th century, notably to the Brooke family's Sarawak, and in 1888 Brunei became a British protectorate. The discovery of oil at Seria in 1929 transformed its prospects. Brunei declined to join the new Federation of Malaysia in 1963 and gained full independence in 1984. The sultan rules as an absolute monarch under the national philosophy of Malay Islamic Monarchy. Kampong Ayer, a cluster of stilt villages on the Brunei River, is one of the largest water settlements in the world and has been inhabited for centuries.

facts: Angkor was the largest pre-industrial urban centre in the world, sprawling across roughly 1,000 square kilometres.
Cambodia's flag is the only national flag that depicts a building.
Tonlé Sap reverses its direction of flow twice a year as the Mekong rises and falls.
KH.about: Much of Cambodia is a low central basin drained by the Mekong and ringed by uplands: the Cardamom Mountains in the south-west, the Dângrêk escarpment along the Thai border and forested plateaus to the north-east. A short coastline faces the Gulf of Thailand. The tropical monsoon brings a wet season from roughly May to October, flooding the plains that grow the country's rice. Between the 9th and 15th centuries the Khmer Empire dominated much of mainland Southeast Asia. Cambodia became a French protectorate in 1863 and regained independence in 1953. Its darkest period came under the Khmer Rouge between 1975 and 1979, when an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people died from execution, forced labour and starvation. The monarchy was restored in 1993 under a new constitution. Today the population is young, Theravada Buddhism is the dominant faith, and garment manufacturing, agriculture and tourism drive the economy.

facts: China borders fourteen countries, tied with Russia for the most in the world.
The entire country operates on a single time zone despite spanning five geographic ones.
It has more than 100 cities with populations above one million.
CN.about: Seen as a whole, China descends in a series of giant steps from west to east: from the Tibetan Plateau, averaging over 4,000 metres, through basins and uplands such as the Sichuan Basin and the Loess Plateau, down to the densely farmed eastern plains and coast. The Yangtze, the longest river in Asia, and the Yellow River both rise on the plateau and flow to the Pacific, while the Gobi and Taklamakan deserts dominate the arid north-west. Climates range from subarctic in the far north to tropical on Hainan. A unified Chinese state was first created by the Qin dynasty in 221 BC, and imperial rule lasted until the Qing dynasty fell in 1912. The People's Republic was proclaimed in 1949. Economic reforms launched in 1978 turned China into the world's largest manufacturer and exporter. Most people live in the wetter east, while the vast western regions remain thinly populated.

facts: Nicosia is the last divided capital city in Europe, split since 1974 by a UN buffer zone.
Cyprus is the third largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia.
Copper takes its name from the island, which supplied the ancient Mediterranean world.
CY.about: Two mountain ranges frame Cyprus: the broad Troodos massif in the south-west and the narrow, limestone Kyrenia range along the northern coast, with the dry, fertile Mesaoria plain between them. The Troodos is one of the best-preserved fragments of ancient oceanic crust on land and is studied by geologists worldwide. Summers are long, hot and dry, and water has always been scarce. Strategically placed in the eastern Mediterranean, the island was ruled in turn by Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Crusader kings, Venetians and, from 1571, the Ottomans. Britain took over its administration in 1878, and Cyprus became an independent republic in 1960. Intercommunal violence between Greek and Turkish Cypriots was followed by the de facto division of the island in 1974, with the north under a Turkish Cypriot administration recognised only by Turkey. Cyprus joined the European Union in 2004, and tourism, shipping and financial services dominate its economy.

facts: Archaeological evidence puts winemaking in Georgia at around 8,000 years ago, the oldest known anywhere.
The Georgian alphabet is one of only a handful of writing systems in the world with no close relatives.
Georgia lies on the boundary between Europe and Asia, and is claimed by both depending on the definition used.
GE.about: Between the Black Sea and the high ridge of the Greater Caucasus, Georgia changes character sharply from west to east. The western lowlands of ancient Colchis, setting of the Greek legend of the Golden Fleece, are humid and subtropical, growing tea and citrus fruit, while the eastern valleys are drier and more continental. The Lesser Caucasus rises in the south. Christianity became the state religion in the 4th century, and the medieval kingdom reached its height under Queen Tamar around 1200. From 1801 Georgian lands were progressively annexed by the Russian Empire. A Democratic Republic existed from 1918 until Soviet forces invaded in 1921, and independence was restored in 1991. Abkhazia and South Ossetia are outside the control of the central government, and a brief war with Russia was fought over South Ossetia in 2008. Traditional polyphonic singing is recognised by UNESCO, and tourism and agriculture are important parts of the economy.

facts: India is the most populous country in the world, having passed China in 2023.
It has 22 languages with official status at national level and hundreds more in daily use.
The whole country runs on a single time zone offset by 30 minutes from GMT.
IN.about: Occupying most of the Indian subcontinent, India stretches from the Himalaya in the north across the broad Indo-Gangetic Plain to the triangular Deccan Plateau, flanked by the Western and Eastern Ghats. The Thar Desert lies in the north-west, and the mainland coast runs for thousands of kilometres along the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. The south-west monsoon, arriving around June, delivers most of the year's rain and remains vital to farming. The Indus Valley Civilisation flourished here more than 4,000 years ago, and later empires such as the Mauryas, Guptas and Mughals left a deep imprint. After nearly two centuries of British dominance, India became independent on 15 August 1947, amid a partition that created Pakistan and displaced millions. Its constitution took effect in 1950, making it a republic and, by electorate size, the world's largest democracy. Information technology services have grown rapidly, though agriculture still employs a large share of workers.

facts: Indonesia is made up of over 17,000 islands, around 6,000 of which are inhabited.
It sits on the Ring of Fire and has more active volcanoes than any other country.
The government is moving the capital from Jakarta, which is sinking, to a new city called Nusantara in Borneo.
ID.about: Straddling the equator for about 5,000 kilometres between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, Indonesia bridges two biological worlds. The Wallace Line, running between Bali and Lombok and between Borneo and Sulawesi, separates species of Asian origin from those of Australasian origin, and the islands are home to unique animals such as the Komodo dragon and the orangutan. Powerful Hindu-Buddhist and later Islamic kingdoms rose here, including Srivijaya and Majapahit, and Borobudur on Java dates from the 9th century. The Dutch gradually brought the archipelago under colonial control from the 17th century. Independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945 and recognised by the Netherlands in 1949 after a bitter struggle. Hundreds of ethnic groups are united by Indonesian, a standardised form of Malay. Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population, and more than half of all Indonesians live on Java. It is the leading producer of palm oil and a major source of nickel.

facts: Damavand is the highest volcano in Asia and the highest peak in the Middle East.
Iran's qanats, underground channels that carry water across desert, have been in use for nearly 3,000 years.
Persian is an Indo-European language, unlike Arabic, which belongs to the Semitic family.
IR.about: Iran is essentially a high plateau enclosed by mountains: the long Zagros chain runs down the west and south-west, and the Alborz range walls off the north, separating the arid interior from the humid, forested Caspian shore. The centre and east are occupied by two great deserts, the salt-crusted Dasht-e Kavir and the Dasht-e Lut, where satellites have recorded some of the hottest land-surface temperatures on Earth. In the 6th century BC Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire, whose ceremonial capital Persepolis still stands in ruins. Later the Sasanians ruled until the Arab conquest in the 7th century, and the Safavid dynasty, from 1501, made Shia Islam the state religion. Although never formally colonised, the country was internationally known as Persia until 1935. The 1979 revolution replaced the monarchy with an Islamic Republic. Iran holds some of the world's largest natural gas reserves, and its population is young and largely urban.

facts: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates is Mesopotamia, where the earliest known cities and writing systems appeared.
Iraq holds some of the largest proven oil reserves in the world.
The Mesopotamian Marshes, drained in the 1990s, have been partially re-flooded and are now a World Heritage Site.
IQ.about: The Tigris and Euphrates both flow south-east through Iraq before joining to form the Shatt al-Arab, which reaches the Gulf along a very short coastline near Basra. North of the alluvial plain, the land rises into the Zagros foothills of the Kurdish north, while a vast stony desert stretches west towards Syria, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Summer temperatures in the south often exceed 50°C. Babylon and Assyria rose here, and from 762 Baghdad was the Abbasid capital and one of the greatest centres of learning of the medieval world. Long a set of Ottoman provinces, the territory came under a British mandate after the First World War, with a monarchy established in 1921 and independence gained in 1932. A republic followed in 1958. War with Iran in the 1980s, the 1991 Gulf War, sanctions and the 2003 invasion left deep scars. The 2005 constitution recognises an autonomous Kurdistan Region, and Arabic and Kurdish are both official languages.

facts: The Dead Sea shore, on Israel's eastern edge, is the lowest land elevation on Earth at around 430 metres below sea level.
Hebrew was revived as an everyday spoken language in the 19th and 20th centuries after centuries of liturgical use.
The country spans a sharp climate gradient, from Mediterranean in the north to desert across most of the Negev in the south.
IL.about: Israel's land falls into a series of narrow north–south strips: a fertile coastal plain on the Mediterranean, hill country in the Galilee and centre, and the deep Jordan Rift Valley to the east. The Sea of Galilee, lying about 210 metres below sea level, is the lowest freshwater lake on Earth and a long-standing source of water. The state was declared on 14 May 1948, as the British Mandate for Palestine ended and following a 1947 United Nations plan to partition the territory. War with neighbouring Arab states followed, and a large Palestinian Arab population was displaced. Many borders remain unresolved, and the status of Jerusalem and of territories occupied in 1967 is contested internationally. Most people live along the coastal plain. Jewish citizens form the majority, while Arab citizens make up around a fifth of the population. Israel has a large technology sector and is known for pioneering drip irrigation and large-scale desalination.

facts: Japan is an archipelago of roughly 14,000 islands, though four of them hold almost the entire population.
About three quarters of the country is mountainous, concentrating cities onto a small share of the land.
Greater Tokyo is the most populous metropolitan area in the world, with around 37 million people.
JP.about: Sitting where four tectonic plates meet, Japan experiences frequent earthquakes and volcanic activity; the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami were among the most powerful ever recorded. The archipelago spans a wide climatic range, from snowy Hokkaido in the north, where cold winds off the Sea of Japan dump heavy snow, to subtropical Okinawa in the south. Its imperial house is the oldest continuing hereditary monarchy in the world, though real power long lay with military shoguns. Under the Tokugawa shogunate, from the 1630s to the 1850s, foreign contact was strictly limited. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 launched rapid modernisation and industrialisation. After defeat in the Second World War, a new constitution took effect in 1947, and Japan became one of the largest economies in the world, famed for cars and electronics. The first Shinkansen high-speed railway opened in 1964. Today Japan has one of the oldest populations anywhere, with nearly three in ten people aged over 65.

facts: Petra, carved into sandstone cliffs by the Nabataeans, was lost to the wider world for centuries before being described by a Swiss traveller in 1812.
Jordan is one of the most water-scarce countries on Earth.
Its only significant coastline is a short stretch on the Gulf of Aqaba at the Red Sea.
JO.about: Most of Jordan is desert plateau, known as the badia, that stretches east towards Iraq and Saudi Arabia. In the west, a band of higher, wetter hills overlooks the Jordan Rift Valley, which drops to the shores of the Dead Sea, while the red sandstone valley of Wadi Rum lies in the far south. The region was part of the Roman world, and Jerash preserves one of the best-kept provincial Roman cities in the Middle East; later, Umayyad rulers built palaces and bathhouses in the eastern desert. After the First World War, the Emirate of Transjordan was created in 1921 under British mandate, with Abdullah I as ruler. It became independent in 1946 and adopted the name Jordan in 1949. The country has absorbed waves of refugees, including Palestinians and, after 2011, Syrians. With few natural resources, it relies on phosphate and potash mining, tourism, services and foreign assistance.

facts: Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country in the world, bigger than all of Western Europe combined.
The Baikonur Cosmodrome, leased to Russia, has launched crewed spaceflights since Yuri Gagarin in 1961.
The Aral Sea, once the fourth largest lake on Earth, has largely dried up through Soviet-era irrigation.
KZ.about: Much of Kazakhstan is open steppe and semi-desert, rising in the south-east to the Tian Shan and in the far east to the Altai. In the west, land around the Caspian Sea dips below sea level, and Lake Balkhash, in the east, is unusual in being largely fresh at one end and salty at the other. Winters are severe and summers hot. The Kazakh Khanate emerged in the 15th century among nomadic herders, and the region was absorbed into the Russian Empire over the 18th and 19th centuries. Soviet collectivisation in the early 1930s caused a famine that killed more than a million Kazakhs, and the Semipalatinsk test site hosted over 450 nuclear tests between 1949 and 1989. Kazakhstan was the last Soviet republic to declare independence, in December 1991. It is the world's largest producer of uranium, a significant oil exporter, with a sizeable ethnic Russian minority in the north.

facts: Kuwait has almost no natural fresh water and relies on desalination for most of its supply.
Its currency, the dinar, is consistently the highest-valued in the world against the US dollar.
Around 90% of the population lives in and around Kuwait City on the coast.
KW.about: Kuwait is almost entirely flat, gravelly desert, its coastline wrapped around the wide inlet of Kuwait Bay at the head of the Gulf. Summers are among the hottest anywhere, with temperatures regularly passing 50°C. On Failaka Island, archaeologists have found remains of a Greek settlement dating from the era after Alexander the Great. The Al Sabah family has ruled since the mid-18th century, when Kuwait grew as a trading port known for pearling and for building wooden dhows. An 1899 agreement placed it under British protection. Oil was struck at Burgan in 1938, one of the largest oilfields in the world, and full independence followed in 1961. In August 1990 Iraq invaded and annexed the country; a US-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces in February 1991, but retreating troops set hundreds of oil wells ablaze. Kuwait's elected National Assembly, founded in 1963, is among the more influential parliaments in the Gulf, and foreign nationals make up about two-thirds of residents.

facts: More than 90% of Kyrgyzstan is mountainous, most of it above 1,500 metres.
Issyk-Kul is the second largest saline lake in the world and never freezes despite the altitude.
Traditional yurt-based herding is still practised in the high summer pastures known as jailoo.
KG.about: Dominated by the ranges of the Tian Shan, with the Pamir-Alay rising along its southern edge, Kyrgyzstan is a country of high valleys, glaciers and fast rivers. The Naryn, its main river, feeds the Toktogul reservoir, whose hydroelectric dams supply much of the nation's electricity. In the south-west, the mountains open onto the edge of the fertile Fergana Valley, where cities such as Osh are concentrated, and the forests at Arslanbob are among the largest natural walnut forests in the world. The Kyrgyz people's heritage is carried by the Epic of Manas, an oral poem far longer than the Iliad and the Odyssey. The area came under Russian control in the 19th century, later became a Soviet republic, and gained independence in 1991. Since then, street protests have toppled governments more than once, in 2005, 2010 and 2020. Gold mining and remittances from workers in Russia form major pillars of the economy.

facts: Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, which is why the Mekong matters so much to its trade and power supply.
It is the most heavily bombed country per capita in history, with unexploded ordnance from the 1960s and 70s still being cleared.
The Mekong forms much of its border and provides most of its electricity through hydropower.
LA.about: Mountains and plateaus cover most of Laos, with the Annamite Range running along the eastern frontier and the most fertile flat land confined to the Mekong lowlands in the west. On the Xieng Khouang plateau, the Plain of Jars holds thousands of large stone jars of prehistoric origin, now a World Heritage Site. The kingdom of Lan Xang, the 'land of a million elephants', was founded by Fa Ngum in 1353 and became a major regional power before splitting into rival kingdoms in the early 18th century. French control was established in the 1890s, and Laos gained independence in 1953. Years of civil war ended in 1975 with the abolition of the monarchy and the founding of the Lao People's Democratic Republic, a one-party state. Theravada Buddhism shapes daily life, and the former royal capital of Luang Prabang is a protected heritage town. A railway linking Vientiane with Kunming in China opened in 2021.

facts: The cedar of Lebanon on the national flag has been prized as timber since antiquity and is mentioned throughout ancient records.
Byblos is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Lebanon's political system allocates the presidency, premiership and speakership to different religious communities.
LB.about: Lebanon is a narrow strip of land where two parallel mountain ranges, Mount Lebanon and the Anti-Lebanon, run close to the Mediterranean. Between them lies the Bekaa Valley, the country's main farming region, drained by the Litani River, which rises and reaches the sea entirely within Lebanese territory. Snow on the high peaks feeds springs and rivers, making Lebanon unusually well watered for the region. Phoenician city-states such as Tyre and Sidon traded across the Mediterranean, and Baalbek preserves some of the largest temples of the Roman world. Under the Ottomans, Mount Lebanon gained special autonomous status in 1861. After the First World War France created Greater Lebanon in 1920, and independence followed in 1943. A civil war from 1975 to 1990 devastated the country, and since 2019 it has suffered a severe financial crisis, compounded by the Beirut port explosion of August 2020. A large diaspora, especially in the Americas, Africa and Australia, sends home vital remittances.

facts: Malaysia is split in two by the South China Sea, with the peninsula on one side and Borneo states on the other.
Putrajaya is the administrative capital, while Kuala Lumpur remains the official one.
Its rainforests are among the oldest in the world, estimated at over 130 million years.
MY.about: Peninsular Malaysia is built around the granite Titiwangsa Mountains, with most cities and plantations on the western side facing the Strait of Malacca, one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world. Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo are more rugged and forested, and the Mulu caves of Sarawak contain some of the largest cave chambers known. The Malacca Sultanate, founded around 1400, controlled the strait's trade until the Portuguese captured the city in 1511; the Dutch and then the British followed. The Federation of Malaya gained independence on 31 August 1957, and Malaysia was formed in 1963 with the addition of Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore, which left in 1965. The population includes Malays, Chinese, Indians and many indigenous peoples of Borneo. Once known for tin and rubber, the economy now centres on electronics, palm oil and natural gas. Uniquely, the king is chosen for five years from among nine hereditary state rulers.

facts: The Maldives is the lowest-lying country in the world, averaging about 1.5 metres above sea level.
It consists of roughly 1,200 coral islands grouped into 26 atolls, with fewer than 200 inhabited.
In 2009 the cabinet held a meeting underwater to draw attention to rising sea levels.
MV.about: Scattered across the central Indian Ocean southwest of Sri Lanka, the Maldives is a chain of atolls built by coral on top of a long submarine ridge, stretching some 800 kilometres from north to south and crossing the equator. The climate is hot and humid all year, shaped by the alternating north-east and south-west monsoons. Islam arrived in the 12th century, and a succession of sultans ruled the islands for most of the following 800 years. Britain treated the archipelago as a protectorate from 1887, managing its foreign affairs while leaving internal rule to the sultanate, until full independence in 1965; the monarchy was abolished in favour of a republic in 1968. Since the first resorts opened in the early 1970s, tourism has become the backbone of the economy, typically with one resort occupying an entire island. Fishing, especially pole-and-line tuna, remains the traditional livelihood, and Dhivehi is written in its own right-to-left script, Thaana.

facts: Mongolia is the most sparsely populated sovereign country in the world.
Ulaanbaatar is the coldest national capital on Earth by average annual temperature.
A significant share of the population still lives nomadically or semi-nomadically in gers.
MN.about: Wedged between Russia and China with no access to the sea, Mongolia spans a broad sweep of high plateau: the Altai ranges in the west, the forested Khangai mountains in the centre, open grassland steppe across much of the east and the gravel plains of the Gobi Desert in the south. Lake Khövsgöl, near the Russian border, holds a large share of the country's fresh water. The climate is sharply continental, with long, severe winters and short summers. In 1206 Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes, and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Later absorbed into the Qing realm, Mongolia declared independence in 1911, became a Soviet-aligned people's republic in 1924, and moved peacefully to multi-party democracy in 1990. Mining, particularly of copper, coal and gold, now drives the economy, while livestock herding remains central to rural life; Mongolian is written mainly in Cyrillic, though the vertical traditional script is being revived.

facts: The capital moved from Yangon to the purpose-built city of Naypyidaw in 2005.
Bagan holds over 2,000 surviving temples and pagodas built between the 11th and 13th centuries.
Myanmar produces most of the world's high-quality rubies, chiefly from the Mogok valley.
MM.about: Myanmar's geography is organised around the Irrawaddy River, which flows the length of the country from the far northern mountains to a broad, fertile delta on the Andaman Sea, long one of Asia's great rice-growing regions. Mountain ranges enclose the central lowlands in a rough horseshoe, with the Rakhine Yoma in the west and the Shan Plateau rising in the east, and the climate is dominated by a heavy south-west monsoon. Powerful kingdoms based at Bagan, Taungoo and later the Konbaung capitals ruled the region before three wars with Britain, ending in 1885, brought it under the British Raj. Administered as a province of British India until 1937, Burma regained independence in 1948, and the military has dominated politics for much of the time since 1962, including after taking power again in 2021. The country officially recognises more than 130 ethnic groups, and long-running armed conflicts in its border hills have shaped its modern history.

facts: Eight of the world's fourteen peaks above 8,000 metres lie wholly or partly in Nepal.
Its flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle or square.
Nepal was never colonised, and its clocks run 45 minutes off GMT, an offset used by no other country.
NP.about: Within a north-south distance of under 250 kilometres, Nepal climbs from the hot, flat Terai, an extension of the Ganges plain lying barely 100 metres above sea level, through the terraced Middle Hills to the high Himalaya. Rivers such as the Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali cut deep gorges southwards through these belts, giving the country considerable hydropower potential. The fertile Kathmandu Valley was home to the Newar city-states whose temples and pagoda-roofed squares are now protected as a World Heritage site. Modern Nepal took shape in the 18th century, when the ruler of Gorkha, Prithvi Narayan Shah, conquered the valley and unified many small hill kingdoms. Hereditary Rana prime ministers held real power from 1846 to 1951, and after a decade-long civil war ending in 2006 the monarchy was abolished and Nepal became a federal republic in 2008. Lumbini, the birthplace of the Buddha, lies in the Terai, and remittances from Nepalis working abroad are a mainstay of the economy.

facts: The Korean Demilitarized Zone separating it from South Korea is among the most heavily fortified borders in the world.
Paektu Mountain, an active volcano on the Chinese border, holds a central place in national mythology.
The country uses its own Juche calendar, counting years from the birth of Kim Il-sung in 1912.
KP.about: Occupying the northern part of the Korean Peninsula, North Korea is predominantly mountainous, with only a small proportion of its land flat enough to farm; most people live on the western coastal plains around Pyongyang and the Taedong River. The Yalu and Tumen rivers trace its long northern border, and winters are markedly colder and drier than in the south of the peninsula. Korea was annexed by Japan in 1910, and after Japan's defeat in 1945 it was divided along the 38th parallel, with Soviet forces occupying the north. The Democratic People's Republic of Korea was proclaimed in 1948, and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953 ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, so the two Koreas remain technically at war. The state has followed an ideology of self-reliance known as Juche, and its centrally planned economy, built on coal, iron ore and other minerals, suffered a severe famine in the 1990s.

facts: Oman controls the southern side of the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the world's seaborne oil passes.
The Musandam Peninsula is an Omani exclave separated from the rest of the country by the United Arab Emirates.
Its aflaj irrigation channels, some over 1,500 years old, still distribute water by gravity across the interior.
OM.about: Oman occupies the south-eastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, with a long coastline facing the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The Al Hajar Mountains arc behind the fertile Batinah coastal plain in the north, while the interior is gravel desert and the dunes of the Wahiba Sands. In the far south, Dhofar catches the summer khareef monsoon, which turns its hills green and supports the frankincense trees that made the region rich in antiquity. Omani sailors were among the great traders of the Indian Ocean: after expelling the Portuguese from Muscat in 1650, Oman built a maritime empire reaching Zanzibar and the East African coast, and for a time its sultan ruled from Zanzibar itself. The Al Said dynasty has governed since the 18th century. Oil exports, beginning in 1967, and rapid modernisation after 1970 transformed the country, which now seeks to diversify through tourism, logistics and fisheries.

facts: K2 is the second highest mountain on Earth and considered far more dangerous to climb than Everest.
The Indus Valley Civilisation, centred on sites such as Mohenjo-daro, was contemporary with ancient Egypt.
Pakistan has the largest glacial ice mass outside the polar regions, in the Karakoram.
PK.about: Pakistan is defined by the Indus, which gathers its waters in the northern mountains, where the Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush converge, and carries them south across the plains of Punjab and Sindh to the Arabian Sea. Fed by its tributaries, the river supports one of the largest contiguous irrigation networks in the world, making the Punjab the country's agricultural heartland. To the west lies the arid, thinly settled plateau of Balochistan, and to the south-east the Thar Desert. The state was created on 14 August 1947 by the partition of British India, accompanied by one of the largest mass migrations in history. It originally comprised two wings separated by India; the eastern wing became independent as Bangladesh in 1971. Islamabad was built in the 1960s to replace Karachi as the capital, though Karachi remains the main port and commercial centre. Punjabi is the most widely spoken first language, and cotton and textiles dominate exports.

facts: Palestine is a UN non-member observer state, recognised by a large majority of member countries.
Its territory is in two separated parts, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
Jericho in the West Bank is among the oldest continuously inhabited settlements known.
PS.about: The two Palestinian territories have very different landscapes. The West Bank is mostly upland, with limestone hills along its spine that fall steeply eastwards into the arid Jordan Valley and the shore of the Dead Sea, the lowest land surface on Earth. The Gaza Strip is a narrow, flat strip of coast on the Mediterranean, about 40 kilometres long and among the most densely populated places in the world. The region was part of the Ottoman Empire for four centuries and came under a British Mandate after the First World War. After the 1948 war, the West Bank was administered by Jordan and Gaza by Egypt; both came under Israeli occupation in the 1967 war. The Palestinian Authority was set up under the Oslo Accords of the 1990s with limited self-government, and since 2007 the two territories have been governed separately. Olive growing is central to both farming and cultural life, and Bethlehem draws pilgrims from around the world.

facts: The Philippines comprises about 7,600 islands, of which roughly 2,000 are inhabited.
It lies on the Ring of Fire and in the main typhoon belt, making it one of the most disaster-exposed countries.
The Philippine Trench off its east coast plunges to over 10,000 metres.
PH.about: Three island groups make up the Philippines: Luzon in the north, the Visayas in the centre and Mindanao in the south. Most of the larger islands are mountainous and volcanic, with narrow coastal lowlands; Mayon is famous for its near-perfect cone, while the Ifugao people of the northern Cordillera carved rice terraces into steep slopes more than two centuries ago. The climate is tropical and maritime, with distinct wet and dry seasons. Ferdinand Magellan's expedition arrived in 1521, and from 1565 Spain colonised the islands, naming them after King Philip II. Filipino revolutionaries declared independence in 1898, but the islands passed to the United States after the Spanish-American War, and full independence followed in 1946 after Japanese wartime occupation. More than three centuries of Spanish rule left a predominantly Roman Catholic population, and English is widely used in government, education and business. Remittances from millions of overseas workers and a large call-centre industry support the economy.

facts: Qatar has the world's third largest natural gas reserves despite its small size.
It is a peninsula with a single land border, and almost the entire population lives in or near Doha.
It hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup, the first held in the Arab world.
QA.about: Projecting north into the Persian Gulf, Qatar is a low, flat peninsula of gravel plains, salt flats and drifting sand, with very little rainfall and no permanent surface water. In the south-east, the Khor al Adaid inlet brings the sea deep among high dunes. For centuries the population depended on fishing and pearl diving, and the collapse of the pearl trade in the 1930s, after cultured pearls reached world markets, brought severe hardship. The Al Thani family has ruled since the mid-19th century, and Qatar became a British protected state in 1916. Oil exports began in 1949, and when Britain withdrew from the Gulf in 1971 Qatar chose full independence rather than joining the federation that became the United Arab Emirates. The offshore North Field, shared geologically with Iran, made it one of the world's leading exporters of liquefied natural gas. Qatari citizens form a small minority of residents.

facts: Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers, the largest country in the world without one.
The Rub' al Khali, or Empty Quarter, is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth.
Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, draw millions of pilgrims each year.
SA.about: Saudi Arabia covers roughly four-fifths of the Arabian Peninsula. Along the Red Sea, the Hejaz and Asir mountains rise steeply from a narrow coastal plain, and the Asir highlands receive enough rain for terraced farming. Inland lies the Najd, a high central plateau, with the red dunes of the Nafud in the north and gravel plains sloping east to the oil-rich coast of the Persian Gulf. Agriculture relies largely on deep, ancient groundwater and desalination. The modern state traces its origins to a 1744 alliance between the ruler Muhammad ibn Saud and the religious reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. After decades of campaigns, Abdulaziz ibn Saud unified the Najd and Hejaz and proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. Oil was discovered near Dammam in 1938, and the Ghawar field is the largest conventional oilfield known. The economy still rests on petroleum, though a long-term plan launched in 2016 aims to expand tourism, industry and services.

facts: Singapore is one of only three surviving sovereign city-states, alongside Monaco and Vatican City.
It has grown around 25% in land area since independence through reclamation.
It has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil.
SG.about: Lying just north of the equator off the tip of the Malay Peninsula, Singapore consists of one main island and around sixty smaller ones, separated from Malaysia by the narrow Johor Strait and linked to it by a causeway and a bridge. The terrain is low and gently undulating, and the equatorial climate brings heavy rain throughout the year with no real dry season. In 1819 Stamford Raffles founded a British trading post here, and its position on the Strait of Malacca turned it into a major entrepôt within the Straits Settlements. Japan occupied the island from 1942 to 1945. Singapore gained self-government in 1959, joined Malaysia in 1963 and became a fully independent republic after separating in 1965. Its port is among the busiest in the world, and finance and manufacturing underpin a highly developed economy. Around four in five residents live in government-built public housing, and limited natural water is supplemented by imports, desalination and recycled water.

facts: Around half of South Korea's population lives in the Seoul metropolitan area.
It went from one of the world's poorest countries in the 1950s to a leading industrial economy within four decades.
Hangul, its alphabet, was purpose-designed in the 15th century rather than evolving gradually.
KR.about: Mountains cover around 70 per cent of South Korea, with the Taebaek range running close to the east coast, so most major rivers, including the Han through Seoul and the Nakdong to Busan, flow west or south. The western and southern coasts are deeply indented, with thousands of islands and wide tidal flats, while the volcanic island of Jeju lies off the south coast. Summers are hot and wet under the monsoon and winters are cold and dry. The Joseon dynasty ruled Korea from 1392 until the late 19th century, and Japan annexed the peninsula in 1910. The Republic of Korea was founded in the US-occupied south in 1948, two years before the Korean War. Decades of authoritarian government gave way to democratic elections in 1987. Large family-controlled conglomerates dominate electronics, shipbuilding and car manufacturing, Korean music, film and television have gained a global audience, and the country has one of the lowest birth rates in the world.

facts: Sri Lanka's administrative capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, though Colombo remains the commercial centre.
It is one of the world's largest tea exporters, a trade established under British rule in the 19th century.
Sigiriya, a palace complex built atop a 180-metre rock column, dates from the 5th century.
LK.about: An island shaped like a teardrop, Sri Lanka is separated from southern India by the shallow Palk Strait and a chain of shoals known as Adam's Bridge. Mountainous highlands in the south-central interior are ringed by plains, and two monsoons divide the island into a wet zone in the south-west and a drier zone covering the north and east. The Mahaweli, its longest river, drains the highlands towards the north-east coast. From the ancient capital of Anuradhapura, early kingdoms built large irrigation reservoirs, known as tanks, many of which are still in use, and Buddhism was established on the island in the 3rd century BCE. The Portuguese, Dutch and British successively controlled the coast, and Britain took the inland Kingdom of Kandy in 1815. Ceylon gained independence in 1948 and adopted the name Sri Lanka in 1972. A civil war between the government and Tamil separatists lasted from 1983 to 2009, and garments, tourism and remittances are now key earners.

facts: Damascus is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Aleppo's ancient souks were one of the largest covered market complexes anywhere before the recent conflict.
The Euphrates crosses the country from Turkey to Iraq and supplies most of its fresh water.
SY.about: Syria has a short Mediterranean coastline backed by a coastal mountain range, behind which the Orontes River flows north through a fertile valley. The Anti-Lebanon Mountains run along the south-western border, while much of the east and south-east is steppe and stony desert. In the north-east, the Jazira plain between the Euphrates and the Khabur is the country's main grain-growing region. The ancient city of Ugarit on the coast produced one of the earliest known alphabets, and the desert oasis of Palmyra was a major caravan city in Roman times. Damascus served as the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750, and the region was ruled by the Ottomans for four centuries. After the First World War it became a French mandate, achieving independence in 1946,. The conflict that began in 2011 displaced around half of the pre-war population, within the country or abroad.

facts: Over 90% of Tajikistan is mountainous, and roughly half of it lies above 3,000 metres.
The Fedchenko Glacier is among the longest glaciers outside the polar regions.
Tajik is a variety of Persian, setting it apart from the Turkic languages of its Central Asian neighbours.
TJ.about: The Pamir mountains dominate eastern Tajikistan, where the region of Gorno-Badakhshan rises into a cold, high plateau with very few inhabitants. Further west, the Zarafshan, Turkestan and Gissar ranges divide the country, so that the northern lowlands around Khujand, on the edge of the Fergana Valley, are separated from the capital and the south-western valleys by high passes. The Panj River, a headstream of the Amu Darya, forms most of the long border with Afghanistan. Fast-flowing rivers provide almost all of the country's electricity, and the Nurek Dam on the Vakhsh is among the tallest in the world. Tajiks regard the Samanid dynasty of the 9th and 10th centuries as the founders of their nationhood. Under Soviet rule Tajikistan became a full union republic in 1929, and after independence in 1991 it endured a civil war from 1992 to 1997. Money sent home by migrant workers, mostly in Russia, is a very large share of national income.

facts: Thailand is the only Southeast Asian country never colonised by a European power.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is among the longest place names in the world.
It is one of the largest rice exporters globally and a major producer of natural rubber.
TH.about: Thailand falls into four broad regions: the forested mountains of the north, the dry Khorat Plateau of the north-east, the fertile central plain watered by the Chao Phraya River, and a long southern arm stretching down the Malay Peninsula between the Andaman Sea and the Gulf of Thailand. The Mekong forms much of the border with Laos. A tropical monsoon climate brings a hot season, a rainy season and a cooler dry season. Thai kingdoms emerged at Sukhothai in the 13th century, and Ayutthaya then became one of the region's major trading powers until it was destroyed by Burmese armies in 1767. The present Chakri dynasty established Bangkok as its capital in 1782. A revolution in 1932 ended absolute monarchy, and in 1939 the country changed its name from Siam to Thailand. Theravada Buddhism is followed by the great majority of the population, and car manufacturing, electronics and tourism are pillars of the modern economy.

facts: Timor-Leste became fully independent in 2002, making it one of the youngest sovereign states.
It occupies the eastern half of Timor island plus the Oecusse exclave inside Indonesian territory.
Portuguese and Tetum are the official languages, a legacy of four centuries of Portuguese rule.
TL.about: Timor-Leste is rugged and mountainous, with a central range running the length of the island so that steep valleys separate the drier north coast, where Dili lies, from the wetter southern lowlands. The island of Atauro, north of the capital, also belongs to the country. Timor lies in Wallacea, the transition zone between Asian and Australian wildlife, and its waters belong to the species-rich Coral Triangle. When Portugal withdrew in 1975, Indonesia invaded and later annexed the territory, a move the United Nations never recognised. Decades of resistance followed, and in a UN-organised referendum in 1999 about four-fifths of voters chose independence; violence after the vote led to a period of UN administration before sovereignty was restored. Revenue from oil and gas fields in the Timor Sea, held in a sovereign petroleum fund, finances most government spending, while high-quality arabica coffee is the main non-oil export.

facts: Istanbul is the only major city in the world spanning two continents, split by the Bosphorus.
Göbekli Tepe in the southeast contains monumental structures older than Stonehenge by roughly 6,000 years.
Turkey controls the Bosphorus and Dardanelles, the sole sea route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
TR.about: Most of Turkey lies on the Anatolian peninsula, a high central plateau enclosed by the Pontic Mountains along the Black Sea and the Taurus Mountains above the Mediterranean, while a small European portion occupies eastern Thrace. Eastern Turkey is the source of both the Tigris and the Euphrates, now harnessed by large dams. The country sits on active fault lines, including the North Anatolian Fault, and has suffered destructive earthquakes, including in 2023. In Cappadocia, erosion of volcanic tuff has produced landscapes of rock cones carved into churches and homes. Anatolia was home to the Hittites, then to Greek and Byzantine civilisations, before the Ottoman Empire grew from a small principality around 1300 into a power spanning three continents. After its collapse, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the Republic in 1923, moving the capital to Ankara and adopting the Latin alphabet in 1928. Turkey is the world's leading hazelnut producer and a major manufacturer of cars and textiles.

facts: The Karakum Desert covers around 70% of Turkmenistan, leaving most of the population along its southern fringe and river oases.
The Darvaza gas crater, alight since the 1970s, is known as the Door to Hell.
Ashgabat holds a record for the highest concentration of white marble buildings of any city.
TM.about: Turkmenistan stretches from the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea to the Amu Darya River, with the Kopetdag mountains rising along the Iranian border in the south. Its climate is sharply continental, with very hot summers and cold winters. Water for farming is carried westwards from the Amu Darya by the Karakum Canal, begun in the 1950s and more than 1,000 kilometres long, one of the longest irrigation canals in the world. The oasis of Merv was among the largest cities of the medieval Islamic world before its destruction by the Mongols in 1221, and its ruins are protected as a World Heritage site. Russian forces conquered the region in the 1880s, and it became a Soviet republic in 1924. After independence in 1991 the country adopted a policy of permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN in 1995. It holds some of the world's largest natural gas reserves, and is renowned for hand-woven carpets and Akhal-Teke horses.

facts: The United Arab Emirates is a federation of seven emirates, formed in 1971.
Abu Dhabi is the capital and holds most of the oil, while Dubai built its economy on trade and services.
Well over 80% of residents are foreign nationals, one of the highest proportions anywhere.
AE.about: Low coastal plains and salt flats line the Persian Gulf shore of the United Arab Emirates, giving way inland to sand desert that merges with the Rub' al Khali around the Liwa Oasis. In the east, the rugged Hajar Mountains separate the interior from a short coastline on the Gulf of Oman. In the 19th century Britain signed a series of maritime truces with the local sheikhdoms, which became known as the Trucial States and remained under British protection until 1971, when they formed the federation; Ras Al Khaimah joined early in 1972. Before oil, the economy depended on pearling, fishing and trade. Abu Dhabi began exporting oil in 1962, funding rapid development. Today Dubai's Jebel Ali port and its airport rank among the busiest in the world, the Burj Khalifa has been the world's tallest building since 2010, and the Barakah plant was the first nuclear power station in the Arab world.

facts: Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, along with Liechtenstein.
Samarkand and Bukhara were among the great trading cities of the Silk Road.
It is one of the world's leading cotton producers, a legacy of Soviet irrigation that helped drain the Aral Sea.
UZ.about: Most of Uzbekistan lies between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, much of it covered by the Kyzylkum Desert, while the autonomous republic of Karakalpakstan occupies the north-west. The population is concentrated in the east, especially in the fertile, densely settled Fergana Valley, ringed by the Tian Shan and Alay ranges, and in irrigated oases along the rivers. Summers are hot and dry and winters can be cold. In the 14th century Timur made Samarkand the capital of a vast empire, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built a renowned astronomical observatory there in the 15th century. Later the region was divided among the khanates of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand until Russian conquest in the 1860s and 1870s. The Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1924, and independence followed in 1991. Central Asia's most populous country, Uzbekistan produces natural gas and is a major gold miner, and much of Tashkent was rebuilt after an earthquake in 1966.

facts: Vietnam is the world's second largest coffee exporter, specialising in robusta.
Hạ Long Bay contains roughly 1,600 limestone islands and islets, most of them uninhabited.
The country stretches over 1,600 kilometres north to south but narrows to under 50 kilometres at its waist.
VN.about: Vietnam's population is concentrated in two great river deltas, the Red River in the north and the Mekong in the south, joined by a narrow coastal strip backed by the Annamite Range along the borders with Laos and Cambodia. Inland lie the basalt plateaus of the Central Highlands. The south is tropical year-round, while the north has a cooler winter season. Northern Vietnam was under Chinese rule for about a thousand years until independence was won in 938, after which Vietnamese dynasties gradually expanded southwards. France colonised the country from 1858 onwards, making it part of French Indochina. Independence was declared in 1945, and after French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954 the country was divided; the Vietnam War ended with reunification under the government in Hanoi in 1976. Market reforms known as Doi Moi, launched in 1986, turned Vietnam into a manufacturing hub and a leading rice exporter. Vietnamese is written in a Latin-based alphabet.

facts: Socotra island hosts hundreds of plant species found nowhere else, including the dragon's blood tree.
Sanaa's old city has been inhabited for more than 2,500 years and is built in distinctive tower houses.
Coffee takes its trade name Mocha from the Yemeni port that first exported it widely.
YE.about: In the south-western corner of the Arabian Peninsula, Yemen rises from the hot, humid Tihamah plain along the Red Sea to high western mountains that catch monsoon rains, making them the wettest part of the peninsula and allowing centuries of terraced farming. Further east, the long Hadramawt valley is known for multi-storey mud-brick towns such as Shibam, and the country overlooks the Bab el-Mandeb strait linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. In antiquity, kingdoms such as Saba grew rich on the incense trade and built a great dam at Marib. In modern times the country developed as two states: the north, ruled by imams until a republic was declared in 1962, and the south, centred on the British-held port of Aden, which became independent in 1967. The two united in 1990. Conflict that escalated in 2014 and 2015 has produced one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises, and water scarcity is a pressing long-term challenge.
